# Overview

Consider the crime data stored in `crime.csv`. We would like to understand how murder rate is related to the other variables in the dataset. Note that `state` is the subject here; it is not a predictor, and `region` is a qualitative variable.

**Task 1.** Build a multiple linear regression model to predict murder rate based on the other variables. The final best model should have all the important variables and it should not have any unimportant variables (use the `anova()` function to compare nested models and to decide which set of predictors can be dropped). Once all the important variables are identified, be sure to explore the significance of pairwise interactions between them as well (using the `anova()` function again). Finally, perform model diagnostics to check the standard model assumptions (normality, constant variance and independence of errors) using the visualization tools (normal QQ plot, residual plot and time series plot) and perform any transformations needed to obtain a model for which the assumptions reasonably hold (e.g. if the variance of errors increases when plotted against fitted values, try transforming y (murder rate) using `log()` or `sqrt()` functions).

**Task 2.** Use your final model to predict murder rate of a state whose predictor values are set at the average in the data for a quantitative predictor and the most frequent category for a qualitative predictor.

# Tidy regression approach

Solve both tasks with the tidymodels workflow from Lab 1 (Linear Regression with {tidymodels}):

- Every model starts from the parsnip specification `lm_spec` and is fit with `fit()`. Do not call `lm()` directly.
- Use `tidy()` to view coefficients and `augment()` to get fitted values and residuals.
- Use `extract_fit_engine()` when a function needs the underlying `lm` object, such as `anova()` and `autoplot()`.
- Use $\alpha = 0.05$ for every test.


# Task 1: Building the model

## 1. Load the packages

```{r}
#| label: q01-load-packages

library(tidyverse)   # readr, dplyr, ggplot2
library(tidymodels)  # parsnip, broom
library(here)        # project-relative file paths
library(ggfortify)   # autoplot() diagnostic plots for lm objects
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not install packages inside this file

If a package is missing, install it from the Tools tab in RStudio or by running the following line in the R Console (not in this file):

`install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "here", "ggfortify"))`
:::

## 2. (2 point) Load and prepare the data

Place `crime.csv` in a folder named `data` inside your RStudio project folder. 

```{r}
#| label: q02-load-data
# Your code here

df <- read_csv('data/crime.csv')

head(df)
```
```{r}
glimpse(df)
```


## 3. (4 point) Specify the model

```{r}
#| label: q03-model-spec
# Your code here
lm_spec <- linear_reg() %>% 
  set_mode("regression") %>% 
  set_engine("lm")
```

## 4. (4 point) Fit the full model

Fit a model named `fit_full` that uses all of the other variables in `crime_df` to predict murder rate. Display its coefficients with `tidy()`.

```{r}
#| label: q04-full-model

# Your code here

#creating model using all variables except state
fit_full <- lm_spec %>% 
  fit(murder.rate ~ . - state, data=df)

#show fit object
fit_full %>%
  pluck("fit") %>%
  summary()

#tidy version
tidy(fit_full)

```


## 5. (10 point) Use `anova()` to drop the unimportant predictors

Two models are nested when the smaller model can be obtained by deleting terms from the larger model. `anova(smaller, larger)` tests whether the deleted terms are needed. A large p-value means the predictor(s) can be dropped.

1. Start from `fit_full`.
2. Choose the predictor with the largest p-value in `tidy()`. 
3. Fit the model without that predictor and compare the two models with `anova()`.
4. If $p > 0.05$, drop the predictor and repeat from the smaller model. If $p \le 0.05$, keep it.
5. Remove one predictor at a time. Stop when every remaining predictor is important.
6. Name the resulting model `fit_main`.


```{r}
#| label: q05-anova-selection

# Your code here
#regionSouth has the highest p-value but it is a dummy variable so trying removing 'region' as a whole
fit_without_region <- lm_spec %>% 
  fit(murder.rate ~ . - state - region, data=df)

#comparing with anova:
anova(fit_without_region %>% 
        pluck("fit"), 
      fit_full %>% 
        pluck("fit"))

```
```{r}
#trying poverty, since it has the next highest p-value
fit_without_poverty <- lm_spec %>% 
  fit(murder.rate ~ . - state - poverty, data=df)

#comparing with anova:
anova(fit_without_poverty %>% 
        pluck("fit"),
      fit_full %>% 
        pluck("fit"))
```
```{r}
#looking at p-values of model without poverty
fit_without_poverty %>%
  pluck("fit") %>%
  summary()

```

```{r}
#removing unemployed
fit_without_poverty_unemployed <- lm_spec %>% 
  fit(murder.rate ~ . - state - poverty - unemployed, data=df)
  
#comparing with fit_without_poverty
anova(fit_without_poverty %>% 
        pluck("fit"),
      fit_without_poverty_unemployed %>% 
        pluck("fit"))
```
```{r}
#examine new p-values
fit_without_poverty_unemployed %>%
  pluck("fit") %>%
  summary()
```
```{r}
#removing college
fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college <- lm_spec %>% 
   fit(murder.rate ~ . - state - poverty - unemployed - college, data=df)
  
#comparing with anova
anova(fit_without_poverty_unemployed %>% 
        pluck("fit"),
      fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college %>% 
        pluck("fit"))
```
```{r}
#examine new p-values
fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college %>%
  pluck("fit") %>%
  summary()
```
```{r}
#removing high.school
fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college_high.school <- lm_spec %>% 
   fit(murder.rate ~ . - state - poverty - unemployed - college - high.school, data=df)
  
#comparing with anova
anova(fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college %>% 
        pluck("fit"),
      fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college_high.school %>% 
        pluck("fit"))
```
```{r}
#examine new p-values
fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college_high.school %>%
  pluck("fit") %>%
  summary()
```
```{r}
#trying again dropping region, since last insignificant p-values come from region dummy variables
fit_with_single.parent_metropolitan <- lm_spec %>% 
   fit(murder.rate ~ single.parent + metropolitan, data=df)
  
#comparing with anova
anova(fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college_high.school %>% 
        pluck("fit"),
      fit_with_single.parent_metropolitan %>% 
        pluck("fit"))
```
```{r}
#assigning final model
fit_main <- fit_without_poverty_unemployed_college_high.school

tidy(fit_main)
```


Record each comparison. Add rows as needed.

| Step | Predictor tested | F | p-value | Decision (drop or keep) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | region | 4.8407 | 0.005749 | keep |
| 2 | poverty | 0.3189 | 0.5754 | drop |
| 3 | poverty & unemployed | 0.9928 | 0.3249 | drop |
| 4 | poverty & unemployed & college | 0.9436 | 0.3369 | drop |
| 5 | poverty & unemployed & college & high.school | 2.5724 | 0.1161 | drop |
| 6 | poverty & unemployed & college & high.school & region | 6.122 | 0.001425 | keep |

**Reflection** Using the p-values from your `anova()` comparisons, explain why each dropped predictor was unimportant.

**Your answer:**
Poverty, unemployed, college, and high.school were unimportant to the model because they did not improve the fit of the lm model. The p-values were above the 0.05 threshold, meaning that we fail reject the null hypothesis that these variables do not have an association with murder rate. Region was a bit tricky because some of the dummy variables seemed statistically insignificant while regionNortheast seemed quite significant from the beginning. After comparing models where region was removed with those where it remains, it eventually becomes clear, however, that region is a variable that we should leave in the final model. 

## 6. (10 point) Explore pairwise interactions with `anova()`

Using only the important predictors in `fit_main`, add one pairwise interaction at a time and compare the model with `fit_main` using `anova()`. Keep any interaction with $p \le 0.05$. If you keep an interaction, also keep its two main effects. Name your model `fit_selected`. If no interaction is significant, `fit_selected` is the same as `fit_main`.

```{r}
#| label: q06-interactions

# Your code here
#checking interaction between single.parent and metropolitan
fit_single.parent_metropolitan <- lm_spec %>% fit(
  murder.rate ~ single.parent*metropolitan + region, data=df)

#comparing with anova
anova(fit_main %>% 
        pluck("fit"),
      fit_single.parent_metropolitan %>% 
        pluck("fit"))

```
```{r}
#checking interaction between single.parent and region
fit_single.parent_region <- lm_spec %>% fit(
  murder.rate ~ single.parent*region + metropolitan, data=df)

#comparing with anova
anova(fit_main %>% 
        pluck("fit"),
      fit_single.parent_region %>% 
        pluck("fit"))
```
```{r}
#checking interaction between metropolitan and region
fit_metropolitan_region <- lm_spec %>% fit(
  murder.rate ~ metropolitan*region + single.parent, data=df)

#comparing with anova
anova(fit_main %>% 
        pluck("fit"),
      fit_metropolitan_region %>% 
        pluck("fit"))
```
```{r}
#none of the interactions were significant so:
fit_selected <- fit_main
```


| Interaction tested | F | p-value | Significant? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| single.parent * metropolitan | 3.6985 | 0.0611 | Not Significant |
| single.parent * region | 0.6879 | 0.5646 | Not Significant |
| metropolitan * region | 0.4997 | 0.6846 | Not Significant |

**Reflection** Which pairwise interactions, if any, are significant? Use the `anova()` results to support your answer and write the formula of `fit_selected`.

**Your answer:**
None of the interactions between the three independent variables proved to be statistically significant, so changing the regression to add interaction variables didn't make sense. The p-values were all above the 0.05 threshold (0.0611, 0.5646, 0.6846, respectively) which means that we fail to reject the null hypotheses that these interactions have an association with murder.rate

## 7. (10 point) Model diagnostics

Check the assumptions of `fit_selected` with the three required plots:

a. Residual plot (residuals vs fitted values) to check constant variance.
b. Normal QQ plot to check normality of the errors.
c. Time series plot of the residuals (residuals in observation order, connected by a line) to check independence of the errors.

```{r}
#| label: q07-diagnostics

# Your code here

# a. Residual Plot
fit_selected_extracted <- extract_fit_engine(fit_selected)
plot(fit_selected_extracted, which = 1)

# b. Normal QQ
plot(fit_selected_extracted, which = 2)

# c. Time series plot of the residuals
residuals_fit <- residuals(fit_selected_extracted)

plot(
  residuals_fit,
  type = "l",
  xlab = "Observation Order",
  ylab = "Residuals",
  main = "Residuals vs. Observation Order"
)

abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)
```


**Reflection** For each assumption (normality, constant variance, and independence of errors), describe what you see in the corresponding plot and state whether the assumption reasonably holds.

**Your answer:**
a. 
From observation of the the plot for the residuals vs fitted, the homoscedasticity assumption holds. The spread of residuals are both above and below the range of fitted values. There is no obvious cone shape, which implies that the residuals are reasonably constant. 

b.
The normality assumption is reasonably satisfied, but some data points may require further investigation. Majority of the data points fall very close to the line, but near the ends there is more deviation. This was also seen in the previous graph. 8, 16, and 18 are possible outliers and may need to be investigated. 

c. 
Overall, there is no clear evidence of dependence of errors from the plot. The residuals do fluctuate above and below zero, however, there are stretches where residuals remain clustered on the positive and negative. However this does not appear to be enough justification to reasonably assume a violation of independence of errors.  

## 8. (5 point) Transform the response if needed

If the variance of the residuals increases with the fitted values, or the QQ plot shows a clear departure from normality, transform the murder rate with `log()` or `sqrt()`.

a. Add the transformed response as a new column in `crime_df`.
b. Refit the model with the same terms as `fit_selected`, using the transformed response.
c. Repeat the three diagnostic plots from Step 7.
d. Name your final model `fit_final`. If no transformation is needed, `fit_final` is the same as `fit_selected`.

```{r}
#| label: q08-transform

# Your code here
fit_final <- lm_spec %>%
  fit(
    murder.rate ~ single.parent + metropolitan + region,
    data = df
  )
formula(extract_fit_engine(fit_final))
```


**Reflection** Which transformation did you use, if any, and why? Do the assumptions reasonably hold for `fit_final`? Write the formula of `fit_final`.

**Your answer:**
From observation of the plots, I do not see any reason to transform the model further. I did could not reasonably assume that any assumptions were violated from observations of the plots. Due to this I will keep the model as it is. I did refit the model, I had some errors in task 10 and this solved it. 

# Task 2: Prediction

## 9. (5 point) Build the typical state

Create a one-row tibble named `typical_state` in which each quantitative predictor equals its average in the data and `region` equals its most frequent category.

```{r}
#| label: q09-typical-state

# Your code here
typical_state <- df %>%
  summarise(
    single.parent = mean(single.parent, na.rm = TRUE),
    metropolitan = mean(metropolitan, na.rm = TRUE),
    region = names(which.max(table(region)))
  )
```


## 10. (4 point) Predict the murder rate

Use `fit_final` and `predict()` to predict the murder rate for `typical_state`. If you transformed the response, convert the prediction back to the murder-rate scale: use `exp()` for a log response, or square the prediction for a square-root response.

```{r}
#| label: q10-prediction

# Your code here
predict(fit_final, new_data = typical_state)

```
**Reflection** Report the predictor values of the typical state and its predicted murder rate on the original scale.

**Your answer:**
The predicted murder rate for a typical state is approximately 5.428. This is based on the average value of the predictors and the most frequent region.
